question: Why are midwives in remote Nigerian health clinics allowed to give certain emergency drugs on their own?

options.A: Doctors are often unavailable during urgent obstetric situations
options.B: Standard hospital policy prohibits doctors from prescribing to newborns
options.C: Midwives complete more medical pharmacology training than doctors
options.D: Pharmacies are legally banned from stocking maternal medications

explanation: You've got this! In remote areas where a doctor might not be around, midwives need the power to act fast and save lives. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h1)

question: What kind of medications are midwives allowed to give independently?

options.A: It changes daily based on the personal preference of the nurse-in-charge
options.B: It includes any drug prescribed traditionally by local birth attendants
options.C: It covers all general medical drugs used in adult emergency medicine
options.D: It is strictly limited to essential maternal and newborn health medications

explanation: Spot on! Midwives stick to their superpower: safe medications specifically for pregnancy, labor, childbirth, and newborn care. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h1)

question: Which body sets the legal scope of practice for Nigerian midwives?

options.B: Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria
options.D: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria

explanation: Great memory! The NMCN is our guiding regulatory body that oversees nursing and midwifery training and practice in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h2)

question: Why are 'standing orders' so important in a rural maternity clinic?

options.A: They give midwives the power to perform major surgical operations independently
options.B: They provide legal authorization for midwives to give specific drugs without a doctor present
options.C: They replace the need for keeping patient health records and drug registers
options.D: They allow patients to purchase restricted medications over the counter without a prescription

explanation: Think of standing orders as your legal safety net—pre-approved protocols that let you step in with emergency treatment right away. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h2)

question: Which drug do you keep on hand to reverse breathing difficulties in a newborn whose mother received strong pain meds during labor?
explanation: Brilliant! Naloxone is an opioid blocker that quickly reverses respiratory depression caused by narcotic pain relief given during labor. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h3)

question: You are getting ready to repair a perineal tear after delivery. Which drug should you draw up to numb the area?
explanation: You got it! Lidocaine is our go-to local anesthetic for numbing the perineum before doing a repair or episiotomy. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h3)

question: What is the first-choice drug to prevent heavy bleeding (postpartum hemorrhage) right after delivery?
explanation: Oxytocin is our superstar first-line defense because it works wonders on the uterus while being gentle on the heart. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h4)

question: Why should you avoid giving ergometrine to a mother with severe high blood pressure?

options.A: It triggers immediate and uncontrollable uterine relaxation
options.B: It completely stops all breast milk production permanently
options.C: It causes a dangerous spike in maternal blood pressure
options.D: It neutralizes the effects of routine postpartum antibiotics

explanation: Exactly! Ergometrine narrows blood vessels, which can dangerously shoot up blood pressure and put a hypertensive mother at risk of stroke. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h4)

question: Which medication is routinely given during antenatal visits to protect pregnant women and babies from malaria?
explanation: Well done! Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) is given at set clinic visits to clear malaria parasites from the placenta and keep the baby safe. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h5)

question: Why do midwives always give iron and folic acid supplements during antenatal care?

options.A: To cure acute bacterial infections of the urinary tract
options.B: To prevent the sudden onset of postpartum hemorrhage after delivery
options.C: To prevent nutritional anemia caused by increased blood volume demands
options.D: To lower elevated blood sugar levels associated with gestational diabetes

explanation: Spot on! Pregnancy increases blood volume, so extra iron and folic acid help build enough red blood cells to keep mom healthy and strong. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h5)

question: Why is vitamin K given as an injection to a newborn baby?

options.A: To treat neonatal jaundice caused by blood incompatibility
options.B: To prevent bleeding disorders due to immature clotting factors
options.C: To stimulate spontaneous crying and lung expansion
options.D: To protect the infant against bacterial eye infections

explanation: You got it! A newborn's tummy is sterile and doesn't make vitamin K yet, so this shot protects them from dangerous bleeding. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h6)

question: After a safe delivery, which eye ointment do you apply right away to protect a newborn from eye infections?
explanation: Brilliant! Tetracycline 1% eye ointment is standard care to shield baby's eyes from harmful bacteria passed during birth. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h6)

question: Why must life-saving drugs like oxytocin be kept in a cold chain (refrigerated)?

options.A: Cold temperatures make the liquid solution taste much sweeter
options.B: Refrigeration prevents the glass ampoules from shattering
options.C: Freezing stops the plastic syringes from melting in storage
options.D: Heat exposure destroys the active potency of the medication

explanation: Exactly right! Uterotonics like oxytocin hate the heat; leaving them out in warm temperatures ruins their strength and effectiveness. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h7)

question: Why should a midwife check her emergency maternity bag on a regular weekly basis?

options.A: To ensure all liquid drugs are transferred into clear glass bottles
options.B: To verify that patient clinical notes are stored inside the drug kit
options.C: To catch expired medications and restock depleted emergency supplies
options.D: To clean the exterior leather surface with strong chemical bleach

explanation: You're thinking like a pro! Regular checks mean you'll never be caught off guard by expired drugs during an emergency. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h7)

question: Which of these details is NOT needed when documenting a medication you gave to a patient?

options.A: The physiological response observed in the patient
options.B: The personal home address of the dispensing pharmacist
options.C: The precise time and date the drug was given
options.D: The exact dosage and administration route used

explanation: Spot on! The pharmacist's address has nothing to do with patient care. Your chart is all about the drug, the time, and how the patient reacted. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h8)

question: What is the very first thing you should do if a patient starts showing signs of an allergic rash after an injection?

options.A: Wait for thirty minutes to see if the rash disappears on its own
options.B: Ask the patient to write down her personal medical history
options.C: Stop the drug administration immediately and provide emergency care
options.D: Transfer the patient to a pharmacy for a replacement drug

explanation: Safety first! Always stop the medication right away to prevent any further reaction, then jump into emergency care. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T11#GNS225_U3_T11_h8)
